avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Any infection in cirrhosis (UTI, pneumonia, cellulitis, SBP, bacteremia) can precipitate HE through cytokine-mediated hepatic dysfunction and increased ammonia production.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. O. is a 52-year-old woman with severe alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C) and prior HE who was brought by her daughter for confusion and inability to arouse over 36 hours. The daughter found her unresponsive in bed. She had been complaining of burning with urination and frequent urination for 4 days; she completed ciprofloxacin 3 weeks ago for a UTI. Temperature 38.4°C, tachycardia 116, hypotension 104/64. Urinalysis shows 3+ bacteria and 2+ WBC. Her ammonia is 168 µmol/L — markedly elevated. She has also been drinking (daughter reports 2 weeks ago). Ascites is present on exam.
